text: An outlier is a value that sits far from the rest of the data. It might be a data-entry mistake, an extra zero typed by accident, an instrument failure, or a legitimate but rare event, like one enormous order from a corporate customer. Outliers matter because they can drag averages, distort charts, and dominate model training. Finding them is mechanical; deciding what they actually are takes judgment.

Here are twelve illustrative order amounts, one of which looks odd. Describe shows a mean of about 130, but a median of just 58.5 — the mean is more than double the median. When the mean sits far away from the median like that, a few extreme values are usually responsible. The median is robust — one wild value barely moves it at all.

The interquartile range, or IQR, is the distance between the 25th and 75th percentiles — here, 51 and 63.5, an IQR of 12.5. The classic rule treats anything more than 1.5 IQRs beyond either quartile as an outlier — that gives fences of about 32.25 on the low end and 82.25 on the high end. Filter for values outside those fences, and only the 940 order shows up. The IQR rule doesn't assume a bell-shaped distribution, which makes it a solid default.

A z-score says how many standard deviations a value sits from the mean. Compute it for every order, and filter for an absolute z-score over 3 — it flags that same 940 order, but notice its z-score is only 3.17, just barely over the common cutoff. The extreme value itself inflates the standard deviation used to judge it, so z-scores can actually miss outliers in small samples. The IQR rule is less affected, because quartiles simply ignore the extremes.

Detecting a value is not the same as removing it — ask what it actually is. If it's an error, like a misplaced decimal or a test record, correct it if you can, or otherwise treat it as missing. If it's real but extreme, keep it, lean on robust statistics like the median, and report results both with and without it. If it's simply too influential for a technique sensitive to extremes, cap it, and document that you did. Never delete a point just because it's inconvenient — that's exactly how analyses become misleading.

Flag it first, then cap it — set is underscore outlier to the mask you built, then clip amount between the low and high fences into a new amount underscore capped column. The 940 order becomes 82.25. Keep the original amount column and the flag right alongside it, so your treatment stays transparent. And the choice genuinely matters: the mean of all twelve orders is 129.83, while the mean excluding that one outlier drops all the way to 56.18.

To recap: a big gap between mean and median is a hint, and describe shows it plainly. IQR fences, 1.5 times the IQR beyond the quartiles, and z-scores beyond 3, are the two standard detection rules. Decide based on what the value actually is — error, real, or too influential. Use clip to cap it, keep the original column, and add a flag. Next: data validation checks.
